1.title: A Faith as Precious as Ours
1.context: The writer names himself Simon Peter, the old name in front of the apostle's name, and tells his readers their faith was received through the righteousness of God and is as precious as the apostles' own. The book stands in the undated group of this series: the letter gives no date for itself, and none is invented for it.
1.question: What does it mean to you that your faith is called as precious as an apostle's?

1.title: Multiplied Through Knowledge
1.context: Grace and peace are wished multiplied, not merely given, and the channel named is the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord. Knowledge in this letter is not information stored but a relationship deepened.
1.question: Where would multiplied grace and peace change your life most right now?

1.title: Everything We Need
1.context: The claim is total: divine power has given everything needed for life and godliness, already, through the knowledge of the one who called us by his own glory and excellence. The calling itself was made by the caller's beauty and worth.
1.question: Do you live as if the supply were complete, or as if something were still missing that you must find elsewhere?

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
1.context: The promises are called precious and magnificent, and their stated purpose is one of the boldest phrases in the New Testament: partakers of the divine nature, attached to the escape already made from the corruption caused by evil desires. The closing paragraph of the episode gathers the foundation whole, as this scene's passage gathers the chapter's first movement.
1.question: What promise of God is doing the most work in your life at the moment?

2.title: Add to Your Faith
2.context: The chain has eight links: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness, and love. Each is added to the one before, and the effort is commanded at full stretch inside a life already furnished by divine power.
2.question: Which link of the chain is weakest in you, and what would adding to it look like this week?

2.title: Not Ineffective or Unproductive
2.context: The danger named is not ignorance but fruitlessness: possessing the knowledge of Jesus and producing nothing with it. The qualities must be possessed and increasing, both, like a field that knows the rain and grows a crop.
2.question: Is your knowledge of Jesus producing anything visible, and what is the crop?

2.title: Nearsighted to the Point of Blindness
2.context: The man without the chain is diagnosed by his eyesight and his memory: nearsighted to blindness because he has forgotten his own cleansing from past sins. In this letter, forgetting is the root disease and reminder is the medicine.
2.question: What have you forgotten about your own cleansing that is costing you your sight?

2.title: A Lavish Reception
2.context: Calling and election are God's side; the practice of the chain is the hearers' side, and two promises attach to the practice: you will never stumble, and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom. The episode's closing summary paragraph is carried in this scene with the promise it rests on.
2.question: What would making your calling and election sure change about an ordinary day?

3.title: I Will Always Remind You
3.context: Reminder is not an apology. The hearers know the truth and are established in it, and the reminders keep coming anyway, because forgetting is a standing danger for people who know.
3.question: What truth do you know well and still need to be reminded of most?

3.title: The Tent Will Soon Be Laid Aside
3.context: The body is pictured as a tent, temporary lodging soon to be struck, and Peter says the Lord made the timing clear to him, without saying how. The letter is his provision for after his departure, written so recall survives the writer.
3.question: If you knew your time was short, what reminder would you spend it writing down?

3.title: Not Cleverly Devised Fables
3.context: The claim is stated as a denial first: the apostles did not follow cleverly devised fables when they made known the power and coming of Jesus Christ. Eyewitness is the word set against fable.
3.question: Where do you treat the coming of Christ as a story rather than a certainty, and what would eyewitness confidence change?

3.title: We Heard This Voice
3.context: The mountain is carried in Peter's own compression: honor and glory, a voice from the Majestic Glory naming the beloved Son, and hearers who were with him on the holy mountain. The Transfiguration is told whole in the Gospel books of this series; this letter stakes the reminder on the hearing. The episode's summary paragraph is carried in this scene.
3.question: What have you heard from God that you could stake your teaching on?

4.title: A Lamp Shining in a Dark Place
4.context: The prophetic word is ranked as confirmed beyond doubt, and the hearers are told to pay attention to it as to a lamp in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in their hearts. The lamp is for the dark, not after it.
4.question: What dark place in your life is the prophetic word meant to be a lamp in right now?

4.title: No Prophecy of Scripture
4.context: The rule is pointed at the prophecy's origin: no prophecy of Scripture comes from one's own interpretation. The prophet was not publishing his own reading of events, and the guard is absolute in form.
4.question: How does knowing prophecy's origin change the way you read it?

4.title: Carried Along by the Holy Spirit
4.context: Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit, the way a ship is carried by the wind in its sails. The initiative is removed from the prophets as firmly as the fables were removed from the apostles. The episode's closing summary is carried in this scene.
4.question: What would it mean to be carried by the Spirit rather than driven by your own will in something you must say?

5.title: Denying the Master Who Bought Them
5.context: False prophets were among the people then and false teachers will be among the hearers now: the danger is inside the congregation. They secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, a phrase left standing at full weight, and the denial ends in swift destruction on themselves.
5.question: Why is secret introduction more dangerous than open attack, and where have you seen it work?

5.title: The Way of Truth Defamed
5.context: Many will follow the depravity, and the watching world will read the way of truth by the people who disgrace it. Peter does not promise that false teaching stays marginal; he tells the beloved beforehand so a crowd is never mistaken for a verdict.
5.question: When have you judged a teaching by the size of its following, and what does this verse say to that?

5.title: Their Destruction Does Not Sleep
5.context: Greed is the engine and deceptive words are the tool, the exploiting of people as a trade. Against the operation stands an old verdict still in force, and a destruction pictured as a living thing that does not doze while it waits. The episode's closing summary is carried in this scene.
5.question: What deceptive words are exploiting people around you, and what does their not sleeping verdict mean for how you respond?

6.title: Chains of Darkness
6.context: The chain of judgments starts at the top of creation: angels sinned and their rank bought them nothing, cast deep into hell and placed in chains of darkness to be held for judgment. The verse is carried in its own words, with no map of the prison added.
6.question: What does it say to you that even angels were not spared?

6.title: A Preacher of Righteousness
6.context: Wrath and rescue sit in the same verse: the ancient world not spared, Noah preserved among the eight. Noah's title here is his preaching. His story stands whole in Genesis in this series; Peter uses it as a pointer, eight preserved out of a world.
6.question: Where do you need to keep preaching righteousness to a world that is not listening?

6.title: Tormented in His Righteous Soul
6.context: Sodom and Gomorrah were reduced to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly, and out of the same fire Lot was rescued, righteous and tormented day after day by the lawless deeds he saw and heard. His torment is his credential: a man at home in Sodom would not have been tormented by it.
6.question: What torments your soul about the place you live, and what does that torment prove?

6.title: The Lord Knows How to Rescue
6.context: The long sentence resolves as knowledge: the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment. Both halves are presented as a demonstrated skill with a record behind it.
6.question: Which half of the Lord's knowing do you need most today: rescue for the godly, or custody for the unrighteous?

7.title: Not Even Angels Dare
7.context: Appetite and contempt are the teachers' two engines. They slander glorious beings freely, while angels, greater in strength and power, dare not bring such charges before the Lord. Reverence here tracks with power rightly understood.
7.question: Where is your tongue bolder than an angel's would be, and what would reverence sound like instead?

7.title: Like Irrational Animals
7.context: The comparison is surrender of reason: creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed, blaspheming in matters they do not understand. Men who run on appetite cannot be followed by people who mean to run on knowledge.
7.question: What appetite in your life is closest to running on instinct rather than on knowledge?

7.title: Hearts Trained in Greed
7.context: Blots and blemishes at the congregation's own table, carousing in broad daylight, eyes full of adultery, seducing the unstable. Trained is an athlete's word turned inside out: hearts that have done their exercises in greed, against the believers told to make every effort in virtue.
7.question: What has your heart been trained in by practice, and what training would retrain it?

7.title: The Way of Balaam
7.context: Balaam son of Beor loved the wages of wickedness, and was rebuked by a speechless donkey that spoke with a man's voice and restrained the prophet's madness. His story stands whole in the Numbers book of this series; Peter gives the teachers his name as ancestor and verdict in one.
7.question: What wages have ever tempted you to bend what you know is true?

8.title: Springs Without Water
8.context: A spring without water and a mist driven by a storm: forms of provision with the provision missing, promises that fail at the moment of need. Blackest darkness is reserved for the men who offer them.
8.question: Where have you drunk from a spring that turned out to be empty, and what did it teach you about testing the water?

8.title: A Slave to Whatever Has Mastered Him
8.context: Lofty but empty words entice those just escaping, promising freedom from teachers who are themselves slaves of depravity. The test of a liberator is his own chains: a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.
8.question: What has mastered you in the past that still tries to sell itself as freedom?

8.title: Worse Than at First
8.context: The chapter's hardest sentence stands at full strength: better not to have known the way of righteousness than to know it and turn away. Knowledge refused after knowledge received is treated as heavier than the first not knowing, because the turning is deliberate.
8.question: What do you know that you are in danger of turning away from, and what would holding on require?

8.title: The Dog and the Sow
8.context: Two farm proverbs close the chapter, one from the book of Proverbs and one from the farmyard, set side by side: the dog returning to its vomit, the washed sow back to her wallowing in the mud. The washing was real, and so is the going back.
8.question: What mud have you been washed from that still draws you, and what keeps you out of it?

9.title: My Second Letter to You
9.context: Peter calls this his second letter to the beloved, both letters reminders meant to stir wholesome thinking by recalling what the holy prophets foretold and the Lord and Savior commanded through the apostles. The line is carried exactly as written, with nothing built on it beyond what the letters themselves say.
9.question: What wholesome thinking most needs stirring in you, and which reminder would stir it?

9.title: Where Is the Promise of His Coming?
9.context: The scoffers are quoted in their own words, an argument from sameness: ever since the fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation. Scoffing follows its own evil desires, Peter says, and argues from what it prefers.
9.question: Where does the sameness of your days wear down your expectation, and what does the scoffer's voice sound like in your own head?

9.title: Formed Out of Water and by Water
9.context: The overlooking is deliberate: the earth was formed out of water and by water, and the world of that time perished through the same water in the flood. Sameness is the one thing the record does not show; the world has already been unmade once by the word of God.
9.question: What fact about God's past acts do you most often overlook when the present looks unchangeable?

9.title: Reserved for Fire
9.context: By the same word that formed and flooded, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men. Reserved and kept are custody words: the cosmos is held as competently as the prisoners of chapter 2. The episode's closing rebuttal is carried in this scene.
9.question: How does knowing the present order is reserved change the way you hold it?

10.title: Do Not Let This Escape Your Notice
10.context: The arithmetic runs both directions: with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. The shape comes from the Psalms, where a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday when it is past.
10.question: Which direction of the line do you need more: that your long wait is short to God, or that his day can hold an age?

10.title: Not Wanting Anyone to Perish
10.context: The delay is redefined: not slowness as some understand slowness, but patience with a purpose, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. The waiting is mercy doing its work at the pace of human turning.
10.question: Whose repentance might God's patience be waiting on in your life, possibly your own?

10.title: The Earth and Its Works Will Be Laid Bare
10.context: The Day comes like a thief, unannounced. The heavens disappear with a roar, the elements are destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works are laid bare, carried exactly as this text gives it. The terror is immediately turned into a question about the people hearing it.
10.question: What in your life would you not want laid bare, and what would you do about it before the Day rather than on it?

10.title: Where Righteousness Dwells
10.context: Dissolution becomes a reason for holiness: what kind of people ought you to be, anticipating and even hastening the day, while the elements melt in the heat. Ahead of the fire stands the promise, a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells, not repaired but new.
10.question: What does looking forward to a world where righteousness dwells do to your loves in this one?

11.title: Spotless and Blameless in His Sight
11.context: Make every effort is the virtue chain's own phrase, aimed now at the day of God: be found at peace, spotless and blameless in his sight. The finding is God's; the effort is the hearers'; the sight that matters is his rather than the world's.
11.question: What effort is yours to make so that you are found at peace when he comes?

11.title: Our Beloved Brother Paul
11.context: Peter names Paul our beloved brother, credits his letters to the wisdom God gave him, and places them with the rest of the Scriptures, admitting some parts are hard to understand and that ignorant and unstable people distort them. The sentence is carried exactly as it stands, with no list, dates, or theory built on it.
11.question: What hard part of Scripture have you been tempted to twist or skip, and what would receiving it straight look like?

11.title: Grow in Grace and Knowledge
11.context: Foreknowledge is armor: since you already know these things, be on your guard against being carried away and falling from your secure standing, and grow instead, in the grace and knowledge of the letter's opening greeting. The doxology then takes the last word, glory both now and to the day of eternity, and the episode's closing paragraph on the letter outliving its writer is carried in this scene.
11.question: Are you growing or guarding more these days, and which of the two does this verse ask of you next?
